judged_by: Matched by a Claude Opus 5.5 agent on 2026-11-25; not yet checked by the labeler.

question.note: Spillover onto perceptions of people with records (Q1) and how representation perceptions are affected (Q3). The counter-narrative question (Q2) is not in the claim.
Repeats Q2 (counter-narrative vs ad alone, p.4).
The recommendation to elevate justice-involved voices instead of stigmatizing attacks is C2, placed in the question slot.

central_claim.note: Gives all three parts: harm to perceptions, improved representation, and the counter-narrative's near-removal of the harm ('vastly ameliorated', abstract).

flags.text: Says the paper argues that Democratic Party ads 'spill over to worsen' perceptions, stated as a fact about the campaign. The paper's quoted purpose is to identify 'the potential for spillover harm that may have been caused' and it calls itself preliminary evidence (p.16); the experiment shows the ad stimulus worsened perceptions, not that the campaign did.

evidence.note: Online survey experiment with Democrats on Prolific (E1, without pre-registration or dates). 'Three-arm' is part of E2; the claim gives neither the arms' identities nor the N (those are only in the quote).
Exclusions for attention checks, duplicates and bot screening (E6; reCAPTCHA not named). Final N of 2,439 is part of E2.
Approximately even allocation to three groups 'with specified ns'; the counts are only in the quote and the arms are not named.
Prolific and the July 12-13, 2025 dates: the parts of E1 missing from entry 0.
Eligibility (U.S. residents, fluent English, Democrats) is the sample part of E1. It does not state the consequence needed for L10, and it is in the evidence slot.
Counter-narrative half of E3 (edited Nevada Current excerpt about a formerly incarcerated assemblymember). The mugshot stimulus is not described in this slot.
With/without covariates not mentioned; same call as the earlier judge.

key_findings.note: The quote is pre-registered hypothesis 2A, not the result, but it is in the paper and the claim states the result correctly (p.11).

flags.text: Says the counter-narrative 'greatly reduced support for the ad'. The paper reports a significant decrease of about 0.17 SD (p.11) and never calls it large; of the two support items only explicit support was significant. The quote is hypothesis 1B, not a result.

key_findings.note: F2: counter-narrative shown before the ad improved perceptions (comparison with the ad alone is implied by 'presented before the ad'; magnitude not given). F4 credited with a mild flag for 'greatly'.

Abstract wording ('improved perceived feelings of representation'). The labeler's F3 decision asks for the named outcome (quality of Democratic representation) and the public-service motives result; neither is given.
The quote is hypothesis 1D; the result is supported (p.11).

scope_and_limits.note: Single time point leaves replication and durability open; repeated exposure and behavior are in the next entry.
Persistence, repeated exposure and behavior: all parts of L5 (the single time point is in the previous entry).
Gives the open question about campaign periods without the July 2025 timing; the earlier judge credited the same statement as L6 in full.
Social desirability / Hawthorne effects not ruled out; omits that the manipulation check eases the concern (it is only in the quote).

theoretical_positioning.note: Social categorization theory explaining spillover. Not credited T4: the entry does not say the study carries the theory to a campaign ad and tests its prediction (same call as the earlier judge on a similar entry).

Accurate to p.3 (ref 39, cited to qualify the emotional-mobilization rationale); a cited literature, not a gold framework or stance. 'Positions itself against' is a little strong for one cited sentence but not flagged.

flags.text: Says prior literature claims negative campaign ads help election success and the authors dispute it. The paper cites meta-analytic evidence that does NOT support negative ads aiding election success (p.2, ref 7) and builds on it; the entry inverts what the literature says and the paper's stance toward it, against its own quote.

interlocutor_claim.note: Accurate to p.4 (ref 54: incarceration may shift ideology right; whether it holds outside status-quo messaging 'remains unclear'). Not a gold interlocutor.
